text: Every tool in this lesson is completely legitimate -- signed by Microsoft or Sysinternals, already installed, already expected to run on a managed endpoint. Living off the land means an attacker uses exactly those tools instead of custom malware, for one reason: a scanner has nothing new to flag. The attack isn't in the tool. It's in how it's used -- and that's exactly why catching it takes behavioral detection, not a signature database.

Four LOLBins show up constantly. PowerShell can download and execute payloads entirely in memory, often with encoded, obfuscated arguments. WMI, a legitimate Windows management interface, gets abused to launch processes on remote machines for lateral movement. certutil.exe, officially a certificate utility, has a long-known side ability to download a file from a URL and decode base64 data -- nothing to do with certificates. PsExec, a Sysinternals remote-execution tool, lets attackers push a payload to many machines at once, just like an admin would.

Every one of these binaries was already on disk, already signed, before the attack began. certutil.exe running is certutil.exe running -- there's no new file to hash, no unfamiliar signature to match. certutil -urlcache -split -f followed by a URL is a command-line pattern almost no admin uses for real certificate work, but it's exactly the pattern a signature scanner is structurally unable to tell apart from any other certutil invocation.

An attacker already inside a network runs that certutil command to pull down a second-stage tool, then uses wmic.exe to launch it on three other machines. No new malware was ever written to disk anywhere. A signature scanner sees nothing wrong. EDR flags the certutil command line as a known downloader pattern, flags the WMI call as suspicious remote process creation, and ties both back to the same process lineage from the original foothold -- catching the technique through behavior, not file identity.

What separates legitimate use from an attack is never the file -- it's the command-line arguments, the process lineage, and the context of who's running it and when. Next, we turn from detection to response: what an EDR platform actually lets an analyst do once a host like this one is confirmed compromised, starting with isolating it from the network.
